sections.text: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed without a final overarching agreement after negotiations hit unbridgeable red lines over fossil fuels. A proposed compromise text failed to mention fossil fuels directly, prompting roughly two-thirds of attending countries, including EU member states, to reject it. Oil-producing nations opposed explicit phase-out language and climate finance terms, leading to the longest UN climate summit ending in deadlock.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The breakdown highlights deep geopolitical divisions and raises questions about the effectiveness of the consensus-based COP model. Critics and officials argued that allowing a small group of petrostates veto power over vital climate action undermines global progress. However, supporters noted that despite the summit's failure, renewable energy transitions continue to advance in the real world.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority. Following the judgment, the UK sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders and announced legislation to block aviation fuel exports. Meanwhile, Malaysia announced it would deport thousands of Myanmar migrants and refugees back to their home country.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This ruling marks the first time the court has found a state responsible for genocide. The 2017 military campaign forced over 700,000 Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh. Although Malaysia stated that hosting refugees has created financial and security burdens, the UN warned against returning people to dangerous conditions in Myanmar.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The UK will raise the ruling at the UN Security Council and host a dedicated meeting. In December, Malaysia plans to return 1,500 people by naval ships, with thousands more scheduled to be flown back.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Former Prime Minister Theresa May criticised Prime Minister Andy Burnham for considering further negotiations regarding the European Union, insisting Brexit is finished. Her comments followed Burnham securing a deal with the EU covering food exports, emissions trading, and a youth scheme. Meanwhile, former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair stated the UK should only rejoin the bloc if it reforms its technology policies.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: May warned that reopening EU negotiations consumes excessive government time and distracts from pressing economic and security priorities. However, Burnham described his recent Brussels agreement as mutually beneficial, while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen highlighted the joint potential for technological innovation.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Burnham announced that both sides will hold an informal brainstorming process to explore future relationship options prior to the upcoming UK-EU summit. He did not state that rejoining the EU would be discussed.

gist: The Pentagon criticised Canada for its defence spending and military capabilities.
Canada's defence minister asserted the nation's sovereignty and independence from the US.
Canada plans to increase defence spending to meet future Nato targets.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Pentagon released a memo criticising Canada's defence capabilities and spending history. The document claimed Canada prioritised economic interests over military optimisation and suggested the US has long subsidised Canadian defence. Canada's defence minister, David McGuinty, rejected the criticism, stating that Canada does not report to the United States.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The memo highlights tensions regarding Canada's role as a Nato partner and its military procurement decisions. Friction exists over Canada's potential choice between US-made F-35 jets and Swedish aircraft, which the Pentagon warned could complicate personnel requirements.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Canada has committed to increasing defence spending to 4% of GDP by the end of the decade and 5% by 2035. Meanwhile, Canadian officials are seeking international support for a new defence bank.

stories.title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
stories.standfirst: A new AI-assisted proof seems to be solid, but we're not sure what it tells us.

articles.title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
articles.standfirst: A new AI-assisted proof seems to be solid, but we're not sure what it tells us.

gist: A mathematician used AI to help produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
The proof is currently being verified by the mathematics community.
AI usage in mathematics raises concerns about the loss of human insight.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, announced a proof of the Riemann hypothesis using the AI model Claude. The proof exists in two forms: a rigorous description in the programming language Lean for verification and a description of the underlying logic.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Riemann hypothesis is a significant problem in mathematics with implications for number theory and cryptography. While AI can efficiently generate proofs, mathematicians worry that the opaque reasoning of neural networks may deprive the field of the valuable insights and new tools typically gained through the human process of discovery.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Mathematicians are currently reviewing the proof. It remains unclear whether the AI-generated logic will provide the field with new mathematical understanding or if it will take years for humans to extract meaningful insights from the work.
